sections.category: Moonshot AI releases Kimi K3, a 2.8-trillion-parameter open-weight MoE that tops the Frontend Code Arena, with full weights due July 27

bullets.body: Moonshot AI on July 16 introduced Kimi K3, which it calls the largest open-weight model built to date: a sparse Mixture-of-Experts transformer with 2.8 trillion total parameters that effectively activates 16 of 896 experts through a Stable LatentMoE framework, a native 1M-token context window, an always-on reasoning mode, and native visual understanding. Two in-house architectural changes carry the release — Kimi Delta Attention, a hybrid linear-attention mechanism, and Attention Residuals, a drop-in replacement for standard residual connections that retrieves representations selectively across depth rather than accumulating them uniformly. On benchmarks it took first place on the Frontend Code Arena at 1,679, ahead of Claude Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol and GLM-5.2, and scored around 57 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (fourth of 189 models, level with Claude Opus 4.8 and GPT-5.5). The model is live now via API at roughly $3 per million input and $15 per million output tokens; Moonshot says it will publish the full weights by July 27, making this an API-first debut with an open-weights follow-through rather than a same-day drop. Simon Willison's write-up frames it as another Chinese lab reaching frontier-adjacent results while working around US compute-export limits.

sections.category: Fireworks AI raises a $1.5B Series D at a $17.5B valuation, past $1B ARR and 40 trillion tokens a day, to scale specialized-model inference

bullets.body: Fireworks AI announced a $1.505 billion Series D at a $17.5 billion valuation this week, led by Atreides Management, Index Ventures and TCV with participation from NVIDIA, Lightspeed Venture Partners, Bessemer Venture Partners, Menlo Ventures and others. The company says it has crossed $1 billion in annualized revenue run-rate, up roughly 5x from its prior round, and now serves more than 40 trillion tokens a day — over 95% of them from models specialized on customers' own proprietary data rather than general-purpose frontier endpoints. Its pitch is the managed-inference layer: turning general models into what it calls specialized intelligence on a high-performance serving stack of more than 200 models, with same-day support for new open-weight releases, placing it alongside Together, Baseten and its hosted-inference peers in a category now commanding frontier-scale economics. Proceeds go to compute capacity, engineering headcount and the platform; NVIDIA's presence on the cap table underlines how strategic the serving-and-fine-tuning tier has become as enterprises move from renting frontier endpoints to owning specialized ones.

sections.category: Claude Code ships v2.1.212 with default-on agent-safety limits — hard caps on WebSearch calls and subagent spawns, plus fail-closed Bash permission fixes

bullets.body: Anthropic's Claude Code reached version 2.1.212 on July 17, and the headline additions are agent-safety guardrails rather than features. A new session-wide cap limits WebSearch tool calls to a default of 200 (tunable via CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_WEB_SEARCHES_PER_SESSION) and a per-session cap limits subagent spawns to a default of 200 (CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENTS_PER_SESSION), both described as stopping runaway search and delegation loops, with /clear resetting the budget; /fork now copies a conversation into its own background agent session so a delegated line of work runs without blocking the main thread. The permission-system fixes are the security core: Bash permission checks now fail closed on file-descriptor redirect forms that bash parses differently than the permission analyzer, a permission-check bypass affecting Windows PowerShell 5.1 sessions is closed, and commands longer than 10,000 characters now always prompt instead of auto-running. It is a concrete sign that runaway-loop budgets and fail-closed permission gating — the vocabulary that local fine-tuning tools and MCP-security vendors adopted after this year's agent-exfiltration incidents — are now shipping default-on inside a mainstream coding agent.

sections.category: WAIC 2026 opens in Shanghai with 108 chips and 208 embodied-AI systems on display, spotlighting a domestic-silicon push led by Dongfang Suanxin's HBM-free 14nm DF1000

bullets.body: The 2026 World Artificial Intelligence Conference opened in Shanghai on July 17, running through July 20 with more than 1,100 exhibitors, over 3,000 exhibits and more than 300 global product debuts; organizers count 108 chips, 261 foundation models and 208 embodied-intelligence terminals on the floor, with humanoid service robots among the headline attractions and the show explicitly framed around competition expanding beyond software into computing power and intelligent hardware. The sharpest hardware signal is domestic silicon designed around US export limits: Shanghai startup Dongfang Suanxin, freshly out of stealth, unveiled its DF1000 accelerator built on a mature 14nm node with no HBM, using software-defined design plus 3D-stacked near-memory computing to claim 520 TFLOPS of BF16 and 6.4 TB/s of memory bandwidth — roughly 33% above NVIDIA's H200 on bandwidth, even as raw compute lands near half an H200's — with mass production targeted for end-2026 and a DF2000 promised at twice the performance in the fourth quarter. With more than ten Chinese general-purpose compute-chip vendors exhibiting together, WAIC is this week's clearest single snapshot of China trying to route around leading-edge lithography and HBM through node choice and advanced packaging rather than process shrink.

sections.category: Check Point's AI Security Report 2026 finds AI now runs live intrusions autonomously and flags durable jailbreaks planted in agent config files that reload every session

bullets.body: Check Point published its AI Security Report 2026 this week, and its July 15 analysis reads as a threshold crossing rather than an incremental update: the report argues AI has moved from development aid to live attack operator, documenting intrusions in which AI ran exploitation workflows autonomously — generating thousands of commands across dozens of sessions with minimal human direction — and a case where one operator used AI to produce VoidLink, an 88,000-line command-and-control framework, in under a week. Two structural findings stand out for anyone running agents: attackers increasingly abuse the agentic architecture rather than single prompts, with a durable bypass that plants malicious instructions in configuration files an agent auto-loads across sessions — the kind of repo or context file agents read on a user's behalf — and detections of longer malicious payloads rose roughly fivefold between March and May 2026, approaching 1% of observed prompts. High-risk AI interactions have doubled year-over-year to about 4% of prompts, and trained reviewers correctly flagged AI-generated faces only around 41% of the time. It moves context-file poisoning and autonomous exploitation onto the board alongside the year's Cursor and MCP incidents as operational, at-scale problems rather than lab demonstrations.

sections.category: AI events to plan around now: the AGI Summit hits San Francisco this weekend, AMD Advancing AI follows July 22-23, and the fall Bay Area calendar stacks up across chips, security and dev tracks

bullets.body: The nearest decision is immediate: the AGI Summit runs July 18-19 at the Palace of Fine Arts in San Francisco this weekend, a 200-plus-speaker gathering with Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, Meta and Tesla on the roster, and AMD's Advancing AI 2026 at Moscone West follows on July 22-23, where Lisa Su and partners are expected to detail the Instinct MI450 accelerator and Zen 6 EPYC Venice CPUs. On the AI-chip and infrastructure track the calendar then runs Hot Chips at Stanford August 23-25 (early registration closes July 31) and the AI Infra Summit at the Santa Clara Convention Center September 15-17, covering silicon, AI data centers and physical AI. The AI-security block clusters in early August: Black Hat USA and DEF CON 34's AI Village in Las Vegas August 1-6, SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit in Half Moon Bay August 11-12, OWASP Global AppSec USA in San Francisco November 5-6, and Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series for agent-hijack and MCP-layer defenders. On the developer and data track: Ai4 2026 in Las Vegas August 4-6, Anyscale's Ray Summit August 24-26 in San Francisco, the AI Tinkerers San Francisco meetup in August, the ACM AI Leadership Summit in Atlanta August 30-September 2, The AI Conference at Pier 48 and OpenAI DevDay at Fort Mason both landing September 29 (with the Runway AI Summit the following day), PyTorch Conference North America in San Jose October 20-21, World Summit AI in Amsterdam October 7-8, GitHub Universe October 28-29, AWS re:Invent November 30-December 4, NeurIPS in December, IEEE-RAS Humanoids at the Santa Clara Convention Center December 7-9, and The AI Summit New York December 9-10 closing the year. Near-term actions: decide on the AGI Summit before Saturday, register for AMD Advancing AI ahead of July 22, and lock the July 31 Hot Chips early rate before booking the early-August Las Vegas security block.
